   109	\section{Conclusion}
   110	
   111	The primary discrepancy is a quantifier mismatch in the quotation: the cited
   112	linearity theorem gives average, not pointwise, closeness.  Its use for the
   113	family indexed by $(x,z)$ also requires an explicit finite common-extension
   114	argument.  Both are open formal reductions compatible with the intended
   115	source conclusion.

    10	\title{Documenting Possible Gaps, Counterexamples, and Formalization Deviations}
    11	\author{}
    12	\date{2026-04-29}
    13	
    14	\begin{document}
    15	\maketitle
    16	
    17	\section{Purpose}
    18	
    19	When a formalization relies on a cited mathematical source, the cited source
    20	should remain intact.  It is a source, not an errata file.  If a possible gap,
    21	missing hypothesis, incorrect numerical constant, or other mathematical
    22	discrepancy is found, the matter should be recorded in a separate LaTeX note.
    23	In this repository such notes live under \path{docs/paper-gaps/}.  The same
    24	principle applies when the formal development has already diverged from the
    25	cited source, for instance by changing a statement so that it compiles, or by
    26	using a different mathematical route because an available formal-library theorem
    27	has a slightly different form.  Such a note is a mathematical note first, and a
    28	record of the formalization second: it should be readable by a mathematician or
    29	mathematical physicist who has not followed the issue discussion.
    30	
    31	The note should isolate the mathematical mechanism.  It should say what the
    32	cited source asserts, what the cited results actually imply, where a term or
    33	hypothesis is lost, and what statement the formal development proves instead.
    34	If the formal proof takes a different route, the note should explain the
    35	replacement argument and the hypotheses on which it rests.  This is especially
    36	important when the proof uses a theorem, construction, or convention from
    37	Mathlib which is not part of the cited argument.  In that case the note should
    38	state the Mathlib result in ordinary mathematical language, explain how it is
    39	specialized to the notation of the paper, and compare its hypotheses and
    40	conclusion with the step it replaces.  It should not merely say that \Lean{} did
    41	not accept a proof, that the modified proof compiles, or that a named library
    42	lemma was applied.
    43	
    44	The documents in this directory should themselves follow this standard.  A
    45	policy or template which reads like a checklist will tend to produce checklist
    46	notes; the examples and templates should therefore be written as mathematical
    47	prose.
    48	
    49	\section{Concision and Readability}
    50	
    51	A paper-gap note should be short enough that a reader can understand the issue
    52	in one sitting.  The first page should answer four questions: what the source
    53	uses, how hard the remaining formal work is, what the formalization or audit
    54	checked, and what the current verdict is.  Begin with a short
    55	\emph{At a glance} section when the note concerns an open or recently resolved
    56	formalization task.  That section should estimate the difficulty, the rough
    57	implementation weight, the split between Mathlib reuse and project-local work,
    58	and the key Mathlib APIs or modules.  Use honest ranges, not false precision.
    59	
    60	The \emph{Key theorem forms} section should be Section~2, immediately after
    61	\emph{At a glance}.  Put the theorem forms before the source details so the
    62	reader knows what the formalization is aiming to prove.  After that, keep the
    63	source assertion, the mechanism being checked, the blueprint/formal comparison,
    64	and the conclusion.  Use more sections only when a counterexample or long
    65	derivation genuinely needs room.
    66	
    67	Keep background to the minimum needed for the local point.  Prefer one clear
    68	special case over a general restatement of the surrounding theorem.  Use displayed
    69	equations for the source assertion, the key calculation, and the theorem forms;
    70	avoid displays for traceability data, declaration names, or long lists.  The
    71	blueprint/formal comparison should be compact and should not repeat the theorem
    72	forms.  The section ``Form of the Note'' below specifies where traceability data
    73	belongs; the body should read as mathematical prose, not as a log.
    74	
    75	If the verdict is that there is no mathematical discrepancy, say so plainly and
    76	stop.  Keep the conclusion highly compact, normally under twenty source lines.
    77	If the only remaining work is an implementation task, name it briefly and link
    78	the issue or pull request in a footnote.
    79	
    80	\section{When the Investigation Starts}
    81	
    82	The investigation starts when the obstruction appears to be mathematical rather
    83	than merely formal.  No final judgement is needed at this stage.  It is enough
    84	that, after reading the relevant source and attempting the corresponding formal
    85	statement, the proof seems to require a different scalar, an additional
    86	hypothesis, a different tensor placement, a distinction between two objects which
    87	the prose identifies, or an auxiliary assertion not supplied by the cited
    88	argument.
    89	
    90	The same investigation should also start when such a deviation is discovered
    91	after the fact.  If the existing formal development or informal blueprint has
    92	already changed the statement, strengthened a hypothesis, weakened a conclusion,
    93	inserted an unadvertised lemma, or replaced the cited proof by a different
    94	formal-library argument, the mathematical change should be documented even if all
    95	relevant files already compile.
    96	
    97	At this early stage the purpose is to preserve the question while it is still
    98	local.  The note may later conclude that the matter is only notational, that an
    99	intermediate estimate in the cited source needs a harmless correction, that a
   100	missing hypothesis is genuinely needed, or that no discrepancy remains.  Thus
   101	the trigger is not the severity of the eventual verdict, but the appearance of a
   102	real mismatch between the cited reasoning and the statement that can be
   103	formalized.
   104	
   105	A failed tactic search, a missing formal lemma, or an inconvenient coercion is
   106	not enough.  The obstruction must survive translation back into ordinary
   107	mathematics.
   108	
   109	Sometimes an investigation uncovers an improvement that is not a discrepancy:
   110	the formalization works correctly, but it could be simplified by using an
   111	existing library, replacing a custom type, or adopting a cleaner proof route.
   112	These are not, by themselves, paper-gap notes.  They are action items.  When
   113	such an improvement is identified, open a GitHub issue or pull request that
   114	describes the proposed change.  If the investigation also produces a paper-gap
   115	note, link the issue or pull request from that note: the note records the
   116	mathematical justification, and the issue or pull request drives the
   117	implementation.
   118	
   119	\section{When to Write a Note}
   120	
   121	A note should be written once the source argument and the formal proof no longer
   122	match as mathematical arguments.  This includes, for instance, a numerical
   123	estimate whose constant does not follow from the cited lemma, a displayed
   124	conclusion which uses an unstated hypothesis, or a step in which two objects are
   125	identified although they must remain distinct.  In analytic, algebraic,
   126	probabilistic, or quantum arguments, such distinctions may concern the domain of
   127	a map, the placement of a tensor factor, the type of an outcome, the distinction
   128	between a structure and a substructure, or the scalar carried by an approximation
   129	relation.
   130	
   131	A note is required when an audit finds that a Lean declaration associated with a
   132	source-labelled statement has acquired an extra non-source hypothesis, such as
   133	bridge, residual, repair, producer, or obligation-structure data.  Such a
   134	declaration is temporary proof debt, not a replacement for the source theorem,
   135	and should not be introduced merely to avoid a \verb|sorry|.  The note must say
   136	plainly that the Lean result is conditional, identify the source-faithful theorem
   137	form that remains to be proved, and give the intended obligation discharger or
   138	removal plan.  The blueprint should not mark the source-labelled statement with
   139	\verb|\leanok| by pointing to this conditional helper.
   140	
   141	Changing a Lean theorem away from the statement in
   142	\path{references/ldt-paper/} is strongly discouraged.  A paper-gap note should
   143	not make such a change look routine: it should explain the mathematical
   144	necessity, or else classify the change as proof debt to be removed.
   145	
   146	When an existing conditional helper is audited, the first task is to extract any
   147	argument it already contains into source-faithful lemmas.  If the remaining
   148	bridge hypothesis cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the formal
   149	development should restore the source theorem statement and record the missing
   150	proof obligation explicitly, rather than retaining the strengthened statement as
   151	though it were the paper theorem.
   152	
   153	This requirement is not meant to classify every explicit Lean side condition as
   154	a discrepancy.  Positivity, nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
   155	and denominator nonvanishing hypotheses may be faithful encodings of the domain
   156	in which the paper's theorem is stated.  The note should distinguish such
   157	boundary hypotheses from hypotheses that supply an unproved step of the paper
   158	argument.
   159	
   160	A note is also appropriate when the proof becomes formal only after changing an
   161	intermediate scalar, weakening a conclusion, strengthening a hypothesis, or
   162	inserting an additional lemma which is not simply an expansion of the cited
   163	argument.  These are mathematical changes, even when they are harmless for the
   164	final theorem.  It is likewise appropriate when an available formal-library
   165	theorem proves the needed result under a somewhat different formulation from the
   166	cited source.  In that case the note should be deliberately pedagogical.  It
   167	should explain, in ordinary mathematical language, what the replacement result
   168	says, how it is specialized, which hypotheses are new or differently packaged,
   169	and why the resulting statement is a legitimate substitute for the step in the
   170	cited argument.  If the issue remains open after reasonable attempts, the note
   171	should say what has been checked and what remains unknown.
   172	
   173	\section{Counterexamples}
   174	
   175	If the cited assertion appears to be false, the note should not stop at saying
   176	that the proof cannot be formalized.  It should give the counterexample, or the
   177	smallest relevant part of it, in ordinary mathematical notation.  The example
   178	should be accompanied by enough verification that the reader can see both sides:
   179	the hypotheses of the cited assertion hold, and its conclusion fails.
   180	
   181	When feasible, the counterexample should also be formalized in \Lean{}.  This is
   182	especially valuable when the example is finite, algebraic, computational, or
   183	otherwise small enough that the failure can be checked without reproducing the
   184	whole surrounding theory.  The note should then state the mathematical content
   185	of the checked counterexample and identify the corresponding Lean declaration in
   186	a footnote.  The Lean file is not a substitute for the prose: the prose should
   187	still explain why the example refutes the cited assertion.
   188	
   189	\section{Revision of a Note}
   190	
   191	A paper-gap note may be provisional.  It may begin as soon as the mathematical
   192	obstruction has been isolated well enough to state the question, and it may be
   193	revised as the calculation, the blueprint, or the corresponding \Lean{}
   194	declarations become clearer.  The first version need not know the final
   195	classification, but it should say plainly which mathematical point is known and
   196	which point remains unsettled.
   197	
   198	Later revisions should not make the note into a chronological log.  They should
   199	rewrite the document so that it remains a coherent account of the present
   200	mathematical understanding.  If the verdict changes, the conclusion should state
   201	the current verdict; the linked issue or pull request can preserve the earlier
   202	discussion.
   203	
   204	\section{Form of the Note}
   205	
   206	Each note should stand on its own.  It should give the date, cite the relevant
   207	source article, and provide enough traceability for the reader to locate the
   208	original passage and the project discussion.  GitHub issues and pull requests may
   209	be linked with \verb|\href|, and source files, line ranges, and labels should be
   210	recorded when they help the reader check the claim.  These references should
   211	serve the exposition rather than govern it: the main text should be organized
   212	around the mathematical assertion and its proof.
   213	
   214	The note should introduce its notation before using it.  Symbols for
   215	measurements, tensor factors, approximation relations, and error parameters
   216	should be named in prose.  If an approximation relation is state-dependent, the
   217	state should be named, or its defining expression should be given when this can
   218	be done briefly.  Only after the notation is in place should the note state the
   219	assertion in the cited source, using a bibliographic citation such as
   220	\verb|\cite[Section~...]{...}| when the section or chapter is known.
   221	
   222	Only the relevant hypotheses should be reproduced.  If the question is a scalar
   223	substitution, a missing term, or a missing hypothesis, the note should not quote
   224	a long unrelated part of the proof.  It should give the cited lemma or
   225	proposition in the special case actually used, then display the calculation or
   226	logical implication in which the discrepancy appears.
   227	
   228	Displayed equations should be used with restraint.  They are appropriate for the
   229	source estimate being checked, the cited estimate in the form actually used, and
   230	the calculation where a term or hypothesis appears or disappears.  When a
   231	displayed equation is identified by a source label, the label should appear on
   232	the right of the display, while the surrounding prose refers to the mathematical
   233	assertion itself.  The standard \texttt{amsmath} command \verb|\tag| is the
   234	right mechanism for this; a separate local convention should be introduced only
   235	if the standard mechanism is genuinely insufficient.  For a multi-line aligned
   236	display, tag the individual lines that carry the source information rather than
   237	forcing a long combined label below the equations.  Short
   238	scalar definitions and elementary inequalities should remain inline when the
   239	sentence reads better that way.  As in ordinary mathematical writing, a displayed
   240	formula is part of the surrounding sentence and should be punctuated accordingly.
   241	
   242	Bibliographic entries used only by these notes should live in
   243	\path{docs/paper-gaps/references.bib}.  A new note should ordinarily begin from
   244	\path{docs/paper-gaps/template.tex}, which records the common LaTeX preamble,
   245	the local bibliography, and a model for right-hand source labels in displayed
   246	equations.
   247	
   248	Blueprint prose cites a note like any other source, with
   249	\verb|\cite{gap:<slug>}|; the bibliography entry in
   250	\path{blueprint/src/references.bib} carries the published URL of the note,
   251	whether the note lives in this repository or in another one.  Lean docstrings
   252	and comments use the repository path form \path{docs/paper-gaps/<slug>.tex}.
   253	
   254	The note should then compare the cited source with the informal blueprint, if
   255	there is one, and with the formal statement.  This comparison should be written
   256	in ordinary mathematical prose.  Formal declaration names and source paths should
   257	be supplied only to identify the exact formal statements, and normally belong in
   258	footnotes.
   259	
   260	The conclusion should give a verdict.  It may say that there is no discrepancy,
   261	that the matter is only notational, that an intermediate estimate needs a
   262	harmless correction, that a hypothesis is missing, that there is a theorem-level
   263	gap, or that the question remains open.  The classification should reflect the
   264	mathematics, not the amount of formal work required.
   265	
   266	\section{Decision Principle}
   267	
   268	The formal development should not silently replace the cited assertion by a
   269	different one.  If the formal statement differs from the cited source, the
   270	reason for the difference should be written down.  Conversely, the note should
   271	not overstate the conclusion.  A wrong intermediate scalar is not a fatal gap in
   272	the theorem if the corrected scalar is bounded by the error parameter appearing
   273	in the theorem statement.
   274	
   275	\end{document}

    12	\title{The Cross-Basis Phase in the Extracted Pauli Observables}
    13	\author{}
    14	\date{2026-09-03}
    15	
    16	\begin{document}
    17	\maketitle
    18	
    19	\section{At a glance}
    20	
    21	\begin{itemize}
    22	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Low.  The source drops a nontrivial phase when the
    23	  two binary-basis indices are distinct.
    24	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} One exact multiplication calculation for
    25	  generalized Pauli observables; no robustness estimate changes.
    26	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Finite-sum bilinearity and the field
    27	  trace are standard algebra.  The extracted-observable product form and the
    28	  project's phase convention are project-local.
    29	  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} The generalized Pauli commutation
    30	  relation and nondegeneracy of the trace pairing.  The local correction is
    31	  tracked in \ghissue{19}.
    32	\end{itemize}
    33	
    34	\section{Key theorem forms}
    35	
    36	Let $e_1,\ldots,e_t$ be the fixed self-dual basis of $\mathbb F_q$ over
    37	$\mathbb F_2$.  With the phase convention of the source, generalized Pauli
    38	observables satisfy
    39	\[
    40	  \tau^X(a)\tau^Z(b)
    41	  =(-1)^{\operatorname{tr}(a\mathbin{\cdot}b)}
    42	   \tau^Z(b)\tau^X(a).
    43	\]
    44	Substituting $a=e_j\widetilde u$ and $b=e_{j'}\widetilde v$ gives the exact
    45	relation
    46	\[
    47	  \widetilde X^j(\widetilde u)\widetilde Z^{j'}(\widetilde v)
    48	  =(-1)^{\operatorname{tr}
    49	      (e_je_{j'}(\widetilde u\mathbin{\cdot}\widetilde v))}
    50	   \widetilde Z^{j'}(\widetilde v)\widetilde X^j(\widetilde u).
    51	\]
    52	This formula applies uniformly, whether or not $j=j'$.
    53	
    54	\section{The false dichotomy in the source}
    55	
    56	Lines~1438--1450 of
    57	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex}
    58	identify each extracted observable with a tensor product containing
    59	$\tau^W(e_j\widetilde u)$.  Lines~1451--1456 then claim that the extracted
    60	$X$- and $Z$-observables commute whenever $j\neq j'$
    61	\cite[lines~1438--1456]{Ji2020MIPStar}.  Self-duality gives only
    62	\[
    63	  \operatorname{tr}(e_je_{j'})=0 \qquad (j\neq j').
    64	\]
    65	It does not imply
    66	\[
    67	  \operatorname{tr}(e_je_{j'}s)=0
    68	  \qquad\text{for every }s\in\mathbb F_q.
    69	\]
    70	
    71	Indeed, for distinct $j,j'$, the element $c=e_je_{j'}$ is nonzero.  The trace
    72	pairing is nondegenerate, so there is an $s\in\mathbb F_q$ for which
    73	$\operatorname{tr}(cs)=1$.  Taking vectors whose first coordinates are $1$
    74	and $s$, with all remaining coordinates zero, gives
    75	$\widetilde u\mathbin{\cdot}\widetilde v=s$.  The two extracted observables
    76	then anticommute.  This is a counterexample to the printed cross-basis
    77	commutation assertion.
    78	
    79	When $\widetilde u\mathbin{\cdot}\widetilde v$ lies in the prime field, the
    80	printed distinction is recovered from self-duality.  The chapter quantifies
    81	over arbitrary vectors, however, so that special case does not repair its
    82	statement.
    83	
    84	\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
    85	
    86	The discussion following the product-form calculation in
    87	\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex}, lines~69--95, records
    88	the full phase and notes that the false dichotomy is not used later in the
    89	extraction argument.  A formal theorem may therefore retain the mathematically
    90	correct uniform phase relation with a \textbf{Local fix} marker.  It must not
    91	assert exact commutation merely from $j\neq j'$.
    92	
    93	This correction changes neither the definition of the extracted observables
    94	nor the source-faithful consistency and extraction conclusions.  It repairs an
    95	auxiliary algebraic assertion that is independent of the robustness estimates.
    96	
    97	\section{Conclusion}
    98	
    99	The source's cross-basis commutation claim is false for general
   100	$\widetilde u$ and $\widetilde v$.  The correct relation retains the phase
   101	$(-1)^{\operatorname{tr}(e_je_{j'}(\widetilde u\cdot\widetilde v))}$.
   102	Because the later argument does not invoke the false dichotomy, this is a
   103	local correction rather than an additional hypothesis on the extraction
   104	theorem.

    37	
    38	/-- Pairs of bounded polynomial representatives returned by the global

    40	noncomputable abbrev PolyPair (P : AdmissibleParams) := Poly P × Poly P
    41	
    42	/-- Split the extended coordinate set into the `X` block, the `Z` block, and
    43	the two scalar coordinates.  This is formalization-only coordinate plumbing
    44	for `def:combine-map`, blueprint
    45	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex:445-480`, paper
    46	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:970-989`. -/
    47	def finCombineEquiv (m : ℕ) :
    48	    Fin (2 * m + 2) ≃ ((Fin m ⊕ Fin m) ⊕ Fin 2) :=
    49	  (finCongr (by omega)).trans

    51	      (Equiv.sumCongr finSumFinEquiv.symm (Equiv.refl (Fin 2))))

    53	/-- Embed an `X`-block coordinate into the extended coordinate set. -/
    54	def embX (m : ℕ) : Fin m → Fin (2 * m + 2) :=

    57	/-- Embed a `Z`-block coordinate into the extended coordinate set. -/
    58	def embZ (m : ℕ) : Fin m → Fin (2 * m + 2) :=

     5	# Expanded registers and point measurements
     6	
     7	This module adjoins two EPR pairs to a heterogeneous Pauli-basis-test strategy,
     8	records the four register placements used in the analysis, and defines the
     9	expanded point observables and measurements.
    10	
    11	## References
    12	
    13	The constructions formalize `def:expanded-state`, `def:expanded-observables`,
    14	`def:expanded-point-measurement`, and `def:expanded-point-trace-projection` in
    15	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:760-874`. Their paper source is
    16	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:367-418`.
    17	-/

    27	/-- The six registers `AA'A''BB'B''`, retaining distinct Alice and Bob local
    28	spaces. This is the register index type of `def:expanded-state`, paper
    29	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:367-372`, blueprint
    30	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:760-781`. -/
    31	abbrev SixReg (P : AdmissibleParams) (ιA ιB : Type*) :=
    32	  (ιA × (PauliRegister P × PauliRegister P)) ×
    33	    (ιB × (PauliRegister P × PauliRegister P))
    34	
    35	/-- Equality of six-register indices is supplied by classical decidability for
    36	the register type. This is the index set of `def:expanded-state`; blueprint
    37	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:760-781`. -/
    38	noncomputable instance sixRegDecidableEq (P : AdmissibleParams)
    39	    (ιA ιB : Type*) : DecidableEq (SixReg P ιA ιB) :=
    40	  Classical.decEq _
    41	
    42	/-- Reassociate the tensor product of the strategy state and two EPR states
    43	directly into register order `AA'A''BB'B''` for
    44	`eq:def-psihat`, paper `14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:367-372`. -/
    45	def sixRegShuffle (P : AdmissibleParams) (ιA ιB : Type*) :
    46	    (((ιA × ιB) × (PauliRegister P × PauliRegister P)) ×
    47	        (PauliRegister P × PauliRegister P)) ≃ SixReg P ιA ιB where
    48	  toFun p := ((p.1.1.1, (p.1.2.1, p.1.2.2)),
    49	    (p.1.1.2, (p.2.1, p.2.2)))
    50	  invFun p := (((p.1.1, p.2.1), (p.1.2.1, p.1.2.2)),
    51	    (p.2.2.1, p.2.2.2))
    52	  left_inv p := by cases p; rfl
    53	  right_inv p := by cases p; rfl

    82	abbrev ExpandedLocalSpace (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide) :=

    85	/-- The strategy state tensored with EPR states on `A'A''` and `B'B''`, in the

    87	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:367-372`, blueprint
    88	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:760-781`. -/
    89	noncomputable def psiHat (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) :

    92	  exact
    93	    reindexState (sixRegShuffle P S.toStrategy.ιA S.toStrategy.ιB)

    98	/-- Place an operator on one of `AA'`, `BA''`, `BB'`, or `AB''`, with the

   102	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:876-922`. -/
   103	noncomputable def place (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (p : Placement)
   104	    (O : Op (S.ExpandedLocalSpace p.side)) :
   105	    Op (SixReg P S.toStrategy.ιA S.toStrategy.ιB) :=
   106	  fun i j =>
   107	    match p with
   108	    | .AA' =>
   109	        O (i.1.1, i.1.2.1) (j.1.1, j.1.2.1) *
   110	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.1.2.2 j.1.2.2 *
   111	          (1 : Op S.toStrategy.ιB) i.2.1 j.2.1 *
   112	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.2.2.1 j.2.2.1 *
   113	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.2.2.2 j.2.2.2
   114	    | .BA'' =>
   115	        (1 : Op S.toStrategy.ιA) i.1.1 j.1.1 *
   116	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.1.2.1 j.1.2.1 *
   117	          O (i.2.1, i.1.2.2) (j.2.1, j.1.2.2) *
   118	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.2.2.1 j.2.2.1 *
   119	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.2.2.2 j.2.2.2
   120	    | .BB' =>
   121	        (1 : Op S.toStrategy.ιA) i.1.1 j.1.1 *
   122	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.1.2.1 j.1.2.1 *
   123	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.1.2.2 j.1.2.2 *
   124	          O (i.2.1, i.2.2.1) (j.2.1, j.2.2.1) *
   125	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.2.2.2 j.2.2.2
   126	    | .AB'' =>
   127	        O (i.1.1, i.2.2.2) (j.1.1, j.2.2.2) *
   128	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.1.2.1 j.1.2.1 *
   129	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.1.2.2 j.1.2.2 *
   130	          (1 : Op S.toStrategy.ιB) i.2.1 j.2.1 *
   131	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.2.2.1 j.2.2.1
   132	
   133	/-- The expanded observable
   134	`W^r(u) tensor tau^W(r * ind_m(u))` on a selected player side. This is
   135	Equation `eq:lc-23`, paper `14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:374-382`,
   136	blueprint `ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:783-807`. -/
   137	noncomputable def expObs (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide)
   138	    (W : PauliKind) (r : PauliScalar P) (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) :
   139	    Op (S.ExpandedLocalSpace side) :=
   140	  heteroKron (S.pointObs side W r u)
   141	    (tauObservable W (fun h => r * indicatorVec u h))
   142	
   143	/-- The Fourier average defining the expanded point effect. This is the first
   144	display of `def:expanded-point-measurement`, paper
   145	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:384-418`, blueprint
   146	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:809-844`. -/
   147	noncomputable def expPointOp (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide)
   148	    (W : PauliKind) (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) (a : PauliScalar P) :
   149	    Op (S.ExpandedLocalSpace side) :=

     5

    42	    [Fintype ιA] [DecidableEq ιA] [Fintype ιB] [DecidableEq ιB]

    73	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:222-244`, paper
    74	`08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:620-652`. -/
    75	def prodShuffle {α β γ δ : Type*} :
    76	    (α × β) × (γ × δ) ≃ (α × γ) × (β × δ) where

     3	/-!
     4	# The low-degree encoding
     5	
     6	This module encodes the Boolean subcube by multilinear indicator polynomials
     7	and packages the resulting low-degree code as honest polynomial representatives.
     8	
     9	## References
    10	
    11	The source-facing nodes are `def:polynomials-degree`,
    12	`def:low-degree-encoding`, and `def:indicator-vector` in
    13	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:321-417`; the paper origin is
    14	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`.
    15	The polynomial class `def:polyfunc` is reused from
    16	`MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries.polyFunc` (the LDT formalization).
    17	-/
    18	
    19	open scoped BigOperators
    20	open MvPolynomial
    21	
    22	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    23	
    24	/- The Boolean cube indexes the `2^m` qudits in the low-degree encoding. -/
    25	/-- The Boolean cube indexing the `2^m` qudits of the test.  This is the index
    26	type in `def:low-degree-encoding`, blueprint
    27	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:381-401`, paper origin
    28	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`.
    29	-/
    30	abbrev Cube (m : ℕ) := Fin m → Bool
    31	
    32	/--
    33	The representative polynomial which is `1` at `y` on the Boolean cube and
    34	zero at the other cube points.  This is the indicator polynomial in
    35	`def:low-degree-encoding` (blueprint lines 381-401; paper
    36	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`).
    37	-/
    38	noncomputable def indicatorPoly {K : Type*} [CommRing K] {m : ℕ} (y : Cube m) :
    39	    MvPolynomial (Fin m) K :=
    40	  ∏ i : Fin m, if y i then X i else (1 - X i)
    41	
    42	/--
    43	The multilinear low-degree encoding of a coefficient string.  Polynomial
    44	representatives are used, as fixed by issue #0004, rather than quotienting by
    45	functional equality.  Blueprint: `def:low-degree-encoding`,
    46	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:381-401`; paper origin:
    47	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`.
    48	-/
    49	noncomputable def lowDegreeEncoding {K : Type*} [CommRing K] {m : ℕ}
    50	    (a : Cube m → K) : MvPolynomial (Fin m) K :=
    51	  ∑ y : Cube m, a y • indicatorPoly y
    52	
    53	/- Evaluation shorthand for the representative polynomial in

1	import MIPStarRE.QPBT.Games.Distance
     2	import MIPStarRE.QPBT.Games.DistributionAux
     3	import MIPStarRE.QPBT.State
     4	
     5	/-! # State-dependent consistency and strategy closeness
     6	
     7	The definitions are the finite-dimensional forms of `def:consistency` and
     8	`def:strategy-distance` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:195-237`,
     9	from `references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-288`.
    10	-/
    11	
    12	open scoped BigOperators
    13	
    14	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    15	
    16	open MIPStarRE.LDT MIPStarRE.Quantum
    17	
    18	/-- The off-diagonal defect in `def:consistency`, blueprint
    19	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:195-208`, paper `06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:232-248`. -/
    20	noncomputable def consistencyDefect {X α ι : Type*}
    21	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
    22	    [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    23	    (μ : Distribution X) (A B : X → α → Op ι)
    24	    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
    25	  avgOver μ (fun x =>
    26	    ∑ a : α, ∑ b : α,
    27	      if a = b then 0 else
    28	        (inner ℂ ψ ((EuclideanSpace.equiv ι ℂ).symm
    29	          ((A x a * B x b).mulVec ψ))).re)
    30	
    31	/-- The quantitative relation in `def:consistency`, blueprint
    32	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:195-208`, paper `06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:232-248`. -/
    33	def IsConsistentWithin {X α ι : Type*}
    34	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
    35	    [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    36	    (μ : Distribution X) (A B : X → α → Op ι)
    37	    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) (δ : ℝ) : Prop :=
    38	  consistencyDefect μ A B ψ ≤ δ
    39	
    40	/-- Unit-alphabet specialization of `def:povm-distance`, blueprint
    41	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:219-226`, paper `06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:258-271`. -/
    42	noncomputable def opDistSq {X ι : Type*}
    43	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    44	    (μ : Distribution X) (M N : X → Op ι) (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
    45	  opFamilyDistSq μ (fun x (_ : Unit) => M x) (fun x (_ : Unit) => N x) ψ
    46	
    47	/-- The unit-alphabet operator distance equals its one-outcome family form from
    48	`def:povm-distance`, blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:219-226`, paper
    49	`06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:258-271`. -/
    50	theorem opDistSq_eq_opFamilyDistSq {X ι : Type*}
    51	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    52	    (μ : Distribution X) (M N : X → Op ι) (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) :
    53	    opDistSq μ M N ψ = opFamilyDistSq μ (fun x (_ : Unit) => M x)
    54	      (fun x (_ : Unit) => N x) ψ := rfl
    55	
    56	/-- The strategy-distance relation `def:strategy-distance`. The two strategies'
    57	local Hilbert spaces are identified, and both measurement distances are
    58	evaluated on the first strategy's state. Blueprint
    59	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:228-237`, paper `06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:273-285`. -/
    60	structure AreCloseStrategies (G : Game) (S S' : Strategy G) (δ : ℝ) : Prop where
    61	  /-- Identification of Alice's local Hilbert spaces. -/
    62	  hA : S.ιA = S'.ιA
    63	  /-- Identification of Bob's local Hilbert spaces. -/
    64	  hB : S.ιB = S'.ιB
    65	  state : stateDistSq S.ψ (reindexState
    66	      (Equiv.prodCongr (Equiv.cast hA).symm (Equiv.cast hB).symm) S'.ψ) ≤ δ
    67	  alice : opFamilyDistSq (G.μ.map Prod.fst)
    68	      (fun x a => heteroKron ((S.A x).effect a) 1)
    69	      (fun x a => heteroKron (reindexOp (Equiv.cast hA) ((S'.A x).effect a)) 1)
    70	      S.ψ ≤ δ
    71	  bob : opFamilyDistSq (G.μ.map Prod.snd)
    72	      (fun y b => heteroKron 1 ((S.B y).effect b))
    73	      (fun y b => heteroKron 1 (reindexOp (Equiv.cast hB) ((S'.B y).effect b)))
    74	      S.ψ ≤ δ
    75	
    76	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

65	
    66	/-- The right marginal of a joint POVM, obtained using `Prod.snd` in
    67	`def:povm-conventions`, `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:8-26`,
    68	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:26-38`.
    69	-/
    70	noncomputable def marginalRight {α β d : Type*}
    71	    [Fintype α] [Fintype β] [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    72	    [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    73	    (M : Measurement (α × β) d) : Measurement β d :=
    74	  M.postprocess Prod.snd
    75	
    76	/-- Projectivity of every effect in a POVM (`def:povm-conventions`, blueprint
    77	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:8-26`; paper origin
    78	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:68-72`). -/
    79	def Measurement.IsProjective {α d : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    80	    (M : Measurement α d) : Prop :=
    81	  ∀ a, IsProj (M.effect a)
    82	
    83	/--
    84	The tensor-product strategy of `def:tensor-product-strategy` in
    85	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:61-69` (paper origin
    86	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:26-38`).
    87	-/
    88	structure Strategy (G : Game) where
    89	  ιA : Type
    90	  ιB : Type
    91	  [ιAFintype : Fintype ιA]
    92	  [ιBFintype : Fintype ιB]
    93	  [ιADecidableEq : DecidableEq ιA]
    94	  [ιBDecidableEq : DecidableEq ιB]
    95	  ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × ιB)
    96	  ψ_norm : ‖ψ‖ = 1
    97	  A : G.QuestionA → Measurement G.AnswerA ιA
    98	  B : G.QuestionB → Measurement G.AnswerB ιB
    99	
   100	attribute [instance] Strategy.ιAFintype Strategy.ιBFintype
   101	  Strategy.ιADecidableEq Strategy.ιBDecidableEq
   102	
   103	/-- The rectangular tensor placement used in strategy probabilities.  This is
   104	the finite-matrix realization of `def:tensor-product-strategy`, blueprint
   105	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:61-69`; paper origin
   106	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:26-38`.
   107	-/
   108	def heteroKron {ιA ιB : Type*} (A : Op ιA) (B : Op ιB) : Op (ιA × ιB) :=
   109	  Matrix.kronecker A B
   110	
   111	/- The Euclidean linear map is the shared action used by the value and distance
   112	functionals.  Keeping it at the Euclidean-space level avoids accidentally
   113	using the function-space supremum norm of `Matrix.mulVec`. -/
   114	/-- Apply a finite matrix to a Euclidean-space state.  This is the Hilbert-space
   115	action underlying `def:tensor-product-value`, paper
   116	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`. -/
   117	noncomputable def applyOperatorToState {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   118	    (M : Op ι) (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι :=
   119	  Matrix.toEuclideanLin M ψ
   120	
   121	/-- The Born weight of an answer pair for a strategy.  Lean-only support for
   122	`def:tensor-product-value`, blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:71-82`, paper
   123	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`. -/
   124	private noncomputable def outcomeWeight {G : Game} (S : Strategy G)
   125	    (x : G.QuestionA) (y : G.QuestionB) (a : G.AnswerA) (b : G.AnswerB) : ℝ :=
   126	  let M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op (S.ιA × S.ιB) :=
   127	    heteroKron ((S.A x).effect a) ((S.B y).effect b)
   128	  let acted := applyOperatorToState M S.ψ
   129	  (inner ℂ S.ψ acted).re
   130	
   131	/--
   132	The tensor-product value, expressed as the distribution average of the Born
   133	probabilities.  This is `def:tensor-product-value` in
   134	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:71-82`, with paper origin
   135	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:40-57`.
   136	-/
   137	noncomputable def Strategy.value {G : Game} (S : Strategy G) : ℝ :=
   138	  avgOver G.μ (fun xy =>
   139	    ∑ a : G.AnswerA, ∑ b : G.AnswerB,
   140	      if G.decide xy.1 xy.2 a b then outcomeWeight S xy.1 xy.2 a b else 0)

  1662	\Cref{eq:qld-sg-cons2} is thus obtained by absorbing $\eps$ into the function $\delta_S$.  
  1663	\end{proof}
  1664		
  1665	
  1666	 The next lemma shows that we can construct local unitaries $V_A,V_B$ from the measurements $\hat{S}$  such that the shared state $\ket{\hat{\psi}}$ is close to $\ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}$ for some state $\ket{\aux}$, and the observables $\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})$ are mapped to Pauli observables $\tau^W(e_j \tilde{u})$ acting on $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}$. Using the consistency between the $\{\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a\}_{a \in \F_q}$ measurements and the points measurements $\{M^{(\Point,W),u}_a\}_{a \in \F_q}$ established in \Cref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis}, and the consistency between the points measurements and the ``total Pauli measurements'' $\{M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h\}_{h \in \F_q^\nqubits}$ established in \Cref{lem:qld-win-implications}, we deduce that the total Pauli measurements must be close (up to the local unitaries $V_A,V_B$) to the Pauli projectors $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^\nqubits}$ acting on $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}$.
  1667	
  1668	
  1669	\begin{lemma}
  1670	\label{lem:qld-unitary}
  1671	There exists a function $\delta_\qld(\eps,m,d,q) = O(\delta_S^{1/4} + md/q)$ (where $\delta_S$ is defined in \Cref{lem:qld-4-7}) and unitaries $V_\alice$ acting on registers $\alice \alice' \alice''$ and $V_\bob$ acting on $\bob \bob' \bob''$ such that 
  1672	\begin{enumerate}
  1673		\item There exists a state $\ket{\aux}$ on registers $\alice \alice' \bob \bob'$ such that
  1674		\[
  1675			\left \| V_\alice \otimes V_\bob \ket{\hat{\psi}}_{\alice \alice' \alice'' \bob \bob' \bob''} - \ket{\aux}_{\alice \alice' \bob \bob'} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}_{\alice'' \bob''} \right \|^2 \leq \delta_\qld.
  1676		\]
  1677		
  1678		\item For all $W \in \{X,Z\}, h \in \F_q^\nqubits$
  1679		\begin{align*}
  1680			V_\alice \, \Big(M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h \Big)_{\alice} \, V_\alice^\dagger &\approx_{\delta_\qld} \Id_{\alice \alice'} \otimes (\tau^W_h)_{\alice''} \\
  1681			 V_\bob \, \Big(M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h  \Big)_{\bob}\, V_\bob^\dagger &\approx_{\delta_\qld} \Id_{\bob \bob'} \otimes (\tau^W_h)_{\bob''}
  1682		\end{align*}
  1683		where the $\approx$ statements hold with respect to the state $\ket{\aux}_{\alice \alice' \bob \bob'} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}_{\alice'' \bob''}$. 
  1684	\end{enumerate}
  1685	\end{lemma}
  1686	
  1687	\begin{proof}
  1688	
  1689	Define the linear map
  1690	\[
  1691		V_\alice = \sum_{g_X,g_Z} (\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z})_{\alice \alice'} \otimes (\tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)))_{\alice ''}\;,
  1692	\]
  1693	where the $\tau^X(\cdot),\tau^Z(\cdot)$ act on $(\C^q)^{\otimes \nqubits}$. (Also note that the argument of $\tau^X$ is $\coded(g_Z)$ and the argument of $\tau^Z$ is $\coded(g_X)$.) We verify the unitarity of $V_\alice$:
  1694	\begin{align*}
  1695		V_\alice V_\alice^\dagger &= \sum_{g_X,g_Z} (\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z})_{\alice \alice'} \otimes (\tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) )_{\alice ''} \\
  1696		&= \sum_{g_X,g_Z} (\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z})_{\alice \alice'} \otimes \Id_{\alice ''} \\
  1697		&= \Id_{\alice \alice' \alice''}
  1698	\end{align*}
  1699	where in the first line we used that the measurement $\{ \hat{S}_{g_\xpt,g_\zpt} \}$  is projective and in the second line we used that the $\tau^Z$ and $\tau^X$ observables are self-inverse. The unitary $V_\bob$ is defined analogously.
  1700	
  1701	Let $\{e_j\}_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}}$ denote the self-dual basis for $\F_q$ over $\F_2$ specified in \Cref{sec:subfields}, and let $\tilde{W}^j$ be the observables introduced in~\eqref{eq:def-tildewj}. Conjugating the observable $\tilde{W}^j$ acting on the registers $\alice \alice' \alice''$ by the unitary $V_\alice$ we get
  1702	\begin{align*}
  1703		&V_\alice \, \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \, V_\alice^\dagger \\
  1704	  =& \sum_{g_X, g_Z} (-1)^{\tr( e_j(\coded(g_W) \cdot \tilde{u}))} \Big( \hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}  \Big)_{\alice \alice'} \otimes \Big ( \tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \\
  1705	  &\hspace{24em}\tau^Z(\coded(g_X))^\dagger \tau^X(\coded(g_Z))^\dagger \Big)_{\alice ''} \\
  1706		 =& \sum_{g_X, g_Z} \Big( \hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}  \Big)_{\alice \alice'} \otimes \Big ( \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \Big)_{\alice ''} \\
  1707		 =& \Id_{\alice \alice'} \otimes \Big( \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \Big)_{\alice ''}\;,
  1708	\end{align*}
  1709	where in the third line we used the (anti-)commutation relation
  1710	\[
  1711		\tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) = (-1)^{\tr( e_j(\coded(g_W) \cdot \tilde{u}))} \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \;.
  1712	\]
  1713	An entirely analogous calculation shows that $V_\bob \, \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \, V_\bob^\dagger = \Id_{\bob \bob'} \otimes \Big( \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \Big)_{\bob ''}$.
  1714	
  1715	Next, from the self-consistency property of the observables $\tilde{W}^j$ specified in \Cref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis} we get that for $W \in \{X,Z\}$,
  1716	\[
  1717		\E_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}} \E_{\tilde{u} \in \F_q^\nqubits} \bra{\hat{\psi}} \left ( \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \otimes \Id - \Id \otimes \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \right)^\dagger \left ( \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \otimes \Id - \Id \otimes \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \right) \ket{\hat{\psi}} \leq \delta_S\;,
  1718	\]
  1719	which, since $\tilde{W}^j$ is Hermitian, is equivalent to
  1720	\begin{equation}
  1721	\label{eq:qld-unitary-1}
  1722	\E_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}} \E_{\tilde{u} \in \F_q^\nqubits} \bra{\hat{\psi}} \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \otimes \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \ket{\hat{\psi}} \geq 1 - \delta_S/2\;.
  1723	\end{equation}
  1724	Let $\ket{\vartheta} = V_\alice \otimes V_\bob \ket{\hat{\psi}}$, and for $W \in \{X,Z\}$ define the operator
  1725	\begin{align*}
  1726		H_W &= \E_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}} \E_{\tilde{u} \in \F_q^\nqubits} \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \otimes \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \\
  1727			&= \E_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}} \Big ( \E_{s \in \F_q} \tau^W(e_j s) \otimes \tau^W(e_j s) \Big)^{\otimes \nqubits} \\
  1728			&= \Big ( \E_{s \in \F_q} \tau^W(s) \otimes \tau^W(s) \Big)^{\otimes \nqubits}
  1729	\end{align*}
  1730	where in the second line we used that for all $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^\nqubits$, $\tau^W(\tilde{u}) = \bigotimes_{i = 1}^\nqubits \tau^W(\tilde{u}_i)$ with $\tau^W(\tilde{u}_i)$ being the generalized Pauli $W$ observable acting on the $i$-th qudit. In the third line, we used the fact that for every fixed $j$, we have $\E_{s \in \F_q} \tau^W(e_j s) \otimes \tau^W(e_j s) = \E_{s \in \F_q} \tau^W(s) \otimes \tau^W(s)$. \Cref{eq:qld-unitary-1} is then equivalent to 
  1731	\[
  1732		\bra{\vartheta} H_W \ket{\vartheta} \geq 1 - \delta_S/2\;,
  1733	\]
  1734	for $W \in \{X,Z\}$. 
  1735	
  1736	Observe that
  1737	\begin{align*}
  1738		\E_{s,s'} \tau^X(s) \tau^Z(s') \otimes \tau^X(s) \tau^Z(s') &= \E_{s,s'} \sum_{a,b \in \F_q} (-1)^{\tr(as')} \ketbra{a+s}{a} \otimes (-1)^{\tr(bs')} \ketbra{b+s}{b} \\
  1739		&= \E_{s} \sum_{a\in \F_q} \ketbra{a+s}{a} \otimes \ketbra{a+s}{a} \\
  1740		&= \proj{\EPR_q}
  1741	\end{align*}
  1742	where to go from the first to the second line we used \Cref{lem:cancellation}. This implies that $H_X H_Z = \Big ( \E_{s,s' \in \F_q} \tau^X(s)\tau^Z(s') \otimes \tau^X(s)\tau^Z(s') \Big)^{\otimes \nqubits} = \ketbra{\EPR_q}{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}$.
  1743	By the triangle inequality, we have
  1744	\[
  1745		\left \| H_X \ket{\vartheta} - H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \right\| \leq \left \| \ket{\vartheta} - H_X \ket{\vartheta} \right\| + \left \| \ket{\vartheta} - H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \right\|\;.
  1746	\]
  1747	Note that for $W \in \{X,Z\}$,
  1748	\[
  1749		\left \| \ket{\vartheta} - H_W \ket{\vartheta} \right\|^2 = 1 - 2\bra{\vartheta} H_W \ket{\vartheta} + \bra{\vartheta} H_W^2 \ket{\vartheta} \leq 2 - 2\bra{\vartheta} H_W \ket{\vartheta} \leq \delta_S\;,
  1750	\]
  1751	where in the inequality we used that $H_W \leq \Id$. Furthermore,
  1752	\begin{align*}
  1753		\bra{\vartheta} H_W^2 \ket{\vartheta} &=\| H_W \ket{\vartheta} \|^2\\
  1754		 &= \| \ket{\vartheta} + (H_W - \Id) \ket{\vartheta} \|^2 \\
  1755		 &\geq (\|\ket{\vartheta}\| - \| (H_W - \Id) \ket{\vartheta} \|)^2 \\
  1756		 &\geq (1 - \delta_S)^2 \\
  1757		 &\geq 1 - 2\delta_S\;. 
  1758	\end{align*}
  1759	Therefore 
  1760	\begin{align*}
  1761	2\sqrt{\delta_S} &\geq \left \| H_X \ket{\vartheta} - H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \right\|^2  \\
  1762	&= \bra{\vartheta} H_X^2 \ket{\vartheta} + \bra{\vartheta} H_Z^2 \ket{\vartheta} - 2\bra{\vartheta} H_X H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \\
  1763	&\geq 2 - 4\delta_S - 2\bra{\vartheta} H_X H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \;,
  1764	\end{align*}
  1765	which implies that 
  1766	\[
  1767		\bra{\vartheta} (\Id_{\alice \alice' \bob \bob'} \otimes (\proj{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits})_{\alice'' \bob''}) \ket{\vartheta} \geq 1 - 2\delta_S - \sqrt{\delta_S} \;.
  1768	\]
  1769	Define the unnormalized state $\ket{\aux_0}$ on the registers $\alice \alice' \bob \bob'$ as
  1770	\[
  1771		\ket{\aux_0}_{\alice \alice' \bob \bob'} = (\bra{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits})_{\alice'' \bob''} \cdot \ket{\vartheta}_{\alice \alice' \alice'' \bob \bob' \bob''}
  1772	\]
  1773	and define the normalized state $\ket{\aux} = \frac{1}{\| \, \ket{\aux_0} \, \|} \ket{\aux_0}$. 
  1774	The inner product between $\ket{\vartheta}$ and $\ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}$ can thus be evaluated as
  1775	\begin{align*}

   832	\subsection{Polynomials and the low-degree code}
   833	\label{sec:ld-encoding}
   834	
   835	In this section, we introduce some basic definitions about polynomials over finite fields. 
   836	An $m$-variate polynomial $f$ over $\F_q$ is a function of the form
   837	\[
   838		f(x_1,\ldots,x_m) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}^m} c_\alpha
   839	  x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_m^{\alpha_m}
   840	\]
   841	where $\{c_\alpha\}$ is a collection of coefficients in $\F_q$.
   842	We say that $f$ has \emph{individual degree (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if
   843	$\alpha_i \leq d $ for all $1\leq i\leq m$, and that it has \emph{total degree
   844	  (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if $\sum_i \alpha_i \leq d$.
   845	(Affine) \emph{multilinear} polynomials are polynomials with individual degree
   846	$1$.
   847	
   848	Low-degree polynomials play an important role in this paper.
   849	For one, the classical and quantum low-degree tests of \Cref{sec:ldt} are
   850	nonlocal games that efficiently certify that the players' answers are consistent
   851	with low-degree polynomials.
   852	Low-degree polynomials are also crucial in the probabilistically checkable
   853	proofs (PCP) construction that are used in ``answer reduction'' transformation
   854	(\Cref{sec:ans}).
   855	
   856	We recall the Schwartz-Zippel lemma: 
   857	
   858	\begin{lemma}[Schwartz-Zippel lemma~\cite{Sch80,Zip79}]
   859	  \label{lem:schwartz-zippel}
   860	  Let $f, g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ be two unequal polynomials with total degree at most $d$. Then
   861	  \begin{equation*}
   862	    \Pr_{x \sim \F_q^m}[f(x) = g(x)] \leq d/q\;.
   863	  \end{equation*}
   864	\end{lemma}
   865	
   866	
   867	\paragraph{The low-degree code.}
   868	The Schwartz-Zippel lemma implies that the set of low-degree polynomials form an
   869	error-correcting code with good distance, which we call the \emph{low-degree
   870	  code}.\footnote{It is also known as the \emph{generalized Reed-Muller code} in
   871	  the coding theory literature.}
   872	
   873	Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$.
   874	For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ define the following $m$-variate multilinear
   875	polynomial over $\F_q$:
   876	\[
   877		\ind_{m,y}(x) = \prod_{i: y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i: y_i = 0} (1 - x_i) \;.
   878	\]
   879	Here, we identify $\{0,1\}$ as a subset of $\F_q$.
   880	Notice that, when restricted to the subcube $\{0,1\}^m$, $\ind_{m, y}$ is zero
   881	everywhere except for when $x = y$.
   882	For $a\in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y\in \{0,1\}^m$
   883	(identifying the latter set with $\{1,\ldots,M\}$ using, say, the lexicographic
   884	ordering on strings).
   885	For any such $a$ define the multilinear polynomial $g_a: \F_q^m \to \F_q$,
   886	called the \emph{low-degree encoding of $a$}, as follows:
   887	\begin{equation}
   888	\label{eq:ld-encoding}
   889		 g_a(x) = \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)\;.
   890	\end{equation}
   891	Note that for any $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, $g_a(y) = a_y$.
   892	Furthermore, the map $a\mapsto g_a$ is linear: for every $x \in \F_q^m$,
   893	\begin{equation}
   894	\label{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}
   895		g_a(x) = a \cdot \ind_m(x)\;,
   896	\end{equation}
   897	where $\ind_m(x)$ is the vector $(\ind_{m,y}(x))_{y \in \{0,1\}^m}\in\F_q^M$.
   898	
   899	\begin{lemma}
   900	\label{lem:ld-encoding-complexity}
   901	Let $q$ be an admissible field size, and let $M = 2^m$ for some integer $m$.
   902	The complexity of computing the evaluation of the low-degree encoding $g_a(x)$,
   903	given $a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$ represented in binary, is $\poly(M,\log
   904	q)$.
   905	\end{lemma}
   906	\begin{proof}
   907		Computing $g_a(x)$ requires computing the sum of products $a_y \cdot
   908	  \ind_{m,y}(x)$ over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$.
   909	  Via \Cref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}, evaluating $\ind_{m,y}(x)$ takes time
   910	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ because it requires performing $m$ multiplications of $\F_q$
   911	  elements, and therefore the product $a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)$ requires
   912	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ time.
   913	  Computing the sum over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ requires $M \cdot \poly(m,\log q)
   914	  = \poly(M,\log q)$ time, as claimed.
   915	\end{proof}
   916	
   917	Finally, for any $H \subseteq \F_q$ we define the \emph{decoding} map
   918	$\coded_H(\cdot)$ which takes as input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and
   919	returns the following vector $a \in \F_q^M$: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, if $g(y)
   920	\in H$, then set $a_y = g(y)$, and otherwise set $a_y = 0$.
   921	Note that for all $a \in H^M$ we have $\coded_H(g_a) = a$ where $g_a$ is the
   922	low-degree encoding of $a$.
   923	For notational brevity we often write $\coded(\cdot)$ to denote the boolean
   924	decoding map $\coded_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.

     4	# Quantitative state and operator distances
     5	
     6	The blueprint uses asymptotic `approx` notation.  The skeleton records the
     7	corresponding squared norm functionals explicitly, leaving universal-constant
     8	estimates to later proof stages.
     9	
    10	## References
    11	
    12	These are `def:state-distance` and `def:povm-distance` in
    13	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:171-220`; the paper origin is
    14	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`.
    15	-/

    18	
    19	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    20	
    21	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    22	open MIPStarRE.Quantum
    23	
    24	/--
    25	Squared Euclidean distance between pure states.  Blueprint `def:state-distance`
    26	(`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:171-179`), paper origin
    27	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`.
    28	-/
    29	noncomputable def stateDistSq {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    30	    [DecidableEq ι]
    31	    (ψ φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
    32	  ‖ψ - φ‖ ^ 2
    33	
    34	/--
    35	Average squared state-dependent distance between two operator families.  This
    36	is `def:povm-distance` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:203-210`,
    37	with paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`.
    38	-/
    39	noncomputable def opFamilyDistSq {X α ι : Type*}
    40	    [Fintype α] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    41	    (μ : Distribution X) (M N : X → α → Op ι)
    42	    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
    43	  avgOver μ (fun x =>
    44	    ∑ a : α, ‖applyOperatorToState (M x a - N x a) ψ‖ ^ 2)
    45

    19	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:195-208`, paper `06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:232-248`. -/
    20	noncomputable def consistencyDefect {X α ι : Type*}
    21	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
    22	    [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    23	    (μ : Distribution X) (A B : X → α → Op ι)
    24	    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
    25	  avgOver μ (fun x =>
    26	    ∑ a : α, ∑ b : α,
    27	      if a = b then 0 else
    28	        (inner ℂ ψ ((EuclideanSpace.equiv ι ℂ).symm
    29	          ((A x a * B x b).mulVec ψ))).re)
    30

    32	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:195-208`, paper `06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:232-248`. -/
    33	def IsConsistentWithin {X α ι : Type*}
    34	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
    35	    [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    36	    (μ : Distribution X) (A B : X → α → Op ι)
    37	    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) (δ : ℝ) : Prop :=
    38	  consistencyDefect μ A B ψ ≤ δ

    41	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:219-226`, paper `06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:258-271`. -/
    42	noncomputable def opDistSq {X ι : Type*}
    43	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    44	    (μ : Distribution X) (M N : X → Op ι) (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
    45	  opFamilyDistSq μ (fun x (_ : Unit) => M x) (fun x (_ : Unit) => N x) ψ
    46	
    47	/-- The unit-alphabet operator distance equals its one-outcome family form from
    48	`def:povm-distance`, blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:219-226`, paper
    49	`06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:258-271`. -/

    51	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    52	    (μ : Distribution X) (M N : X → Op ι) (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) :
    53	    opDistSq μ M N ψ = opFamilyDistSq μ (fun x (_ : Unit) => M x)
    54	      (fun x (_ : Unit) => N x) ψ := rfl

    58	evaluated on the first strategy's state. Blueprint
    59	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:228-237`, paper `06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:273-285`. -/
    60	structure AreCloseStrategies (G : Game) (S S' : Strategy G) (δ : ℝ) : Prop where
    61	  /-- Identification of Alice's local Hilbert spaces. -/
    62	  hA : S.ιA = S'.ιA
    63	  /-- Identification of Bob's local Hilbert spaces. -/
    64	  hB : S.ιB = S'.ιB
    65	  state : stateDistSq S.ψ (reindexState
    66	      (Equiv.prodCongr (Equiv.cast hA).symm (Equiv.cast hB).symm) S'.ψ) ≤ δ
    67	  alice : opFamilyDistSq (G.μ.map Prod.fst)
    68	      (fun x a => heteroKron ((S.A x).effect a) 1)
    69	      (fun x a => heteroKron (reindexOp (Equiv.cast hA) ((S'.A x).effect a)) 1)
    70	      S.ψ ≤ δ
    71	  bob : opFamilyDistSq (G.μ.map Prod.snd)
    72	      (fun y b => heteroKron 1 ((S.B y).effect b))
    73	      (fun y b => heteroKron 1 (reindexOp (Equiv.cast hB) ((S'.B y).effect b)))
    74	      S.ψ ≤ δ
    75	
    76	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

  1770	\[
  1771		\ket{\aux_0}_{\alice \alice' \bob \bob'} = (\bra{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits})_{\alice'' \bob''} \cdot \ket{\vartheta}_{\alice \alice' \alice'' \bob \bob' \bob''}

  1787		\label{eq:qld-unitary-2}
  1788		M^{(\Pauli,W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} \otimes \Id_{\bob \bob' \bob''} &\simeq_\eps \Id_{\alice \alice' \alice''} \otimes M^{(\Point,W),u}_a\;, \\

  1794		\begin{equation}
  1795		\label{eq:qld-unitary-4}
  1796			M^{(\Point,W),u}_a \otimes \Id_{\bob \bob' \bob''} \simeq_{\delta_S} \Id_{\alice \alice' \alice''}  \otimes \tilde{M}^{W,\ind_m(u)}_a\;.

  1799		\begin{equation}
  1800			\label{eq:qld-unitary-5}
  1801			M^{(\Pauli,W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} \otimes \Id_{\bob \bob' \bob''} \simeq_{\sqrt{\delta_S}} \Id_{\alice \alice' \alice''}  \otimes \tilde{M}^{W,\ind_m(u)}_a\;,
  1802		\end{equation}
  1803		where we used that $\delta_S \geq \eps$. 
  1804		
  1805		Next, we have for all $u \in \F_q^m$ 
  1806		\begin{align}
  1807			&V_\bob \, \tilde{M}^{W,\ind_m(u)}_a \, V_\bob^\dagger \notag \\
  1808			= &\sum_{g_X, g_Z} \Big( \hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}  \Big)_{\bob \bob'} \otimes \Big ( \tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \tau^W_{g_W(u) - a}(\ind_m(u))    \tau^Z(\coded(g_X))^\dagger \tau^X(\coded(g_Z))^\dagger \Big)_{\bob ''} \notag \\
  1809			= &\sum_{g_X, g_Z} \Big( \hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}  \Big)_{\bob \bob'} \otimes \sum_{h : g_h(u) = g_W(u) - a} \Big ( \tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \tau^W_h   \tau^Z(\coded(g_X))^\dagger \tau^X(\coded(g_Z))^\dagger \Big)_{\bob ''} \notag \\
  1810			= &\sum_{g_X, g_Z} \Big( \hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}  \Big)_{\bob \bob'} \otimes \sum_{h : g_h(u) = g_W(u) - a} \Big ( \tau^W_{h + \coded(g_W)}   \Big)_{\bob ''} \notag \\
  1811		= &\sum_{g_X, g_Z} \Big( \hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}  \Big)_{\bob \bob'} \otimes \sum_{h : g_h(u) = a} \Big ( \tau^W_{h}   \Big)_{\bob ''} \notag \\
  1812	= &\Id_{\bob \bob'} \otimes (\tau^W_{[g_h(u)=a]})_{\bob''}\;,		\label{eq:qld-unitary-6}
  1813		\end{align}
  1814		where in the second line we expanded out the definitions of $V_\bob$ and $\tilde{M}^{W,\ind_m(u)}_a$ (defined in \cref{eq:tilde_M}); in the third line we expanded out the definition of $\tau^W_{g_W(u) - a}(\ind_m(u))$ (defined in \cref{eq:def-tauwu}) and used the fact that for all $h \in \F_q^M$, the inner product $h \cdot \ind_m(u)$ is equal to $g_h(u)$; in the fourth line we used the identities
  1815		\[
  1816			\tau^X(s) \tau^Z_h \tau^X(s)^\dagger = \tau^Z_{h + s} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \tau^Z(s) \tau^X_h \tau^Z(s)^\dagger = \tau^X_{h + s}~;
  1817		\]

  1819		\begin{align*}
  1820			\sum_{h : g_h(u) = g_W(u) - a}  \tau^W_{h + \coded(g_W)} = \sum_{h: g_W(u) - g_h(u) = a} \tau^W_{h + \coded(g_W)} = \sum_{h: g_W(u) + g_h(u) = a} \tau^W_{h + \coded(g_W)} = \sum_{h': g_{h'}(u) = a} \tau^W_{h'}~.

  1824		
  1825	
  1826	
  1827	Let $\ket{\Delta} = \ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}$. We show that $V_\alice \, \Big(M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h \Big)_{\alice} \, V_\alice^\dagger \approx_{\delta_\qld} \Id_{\alice \alice'} \otimes (\tau^W_h)_{\alice''}$ (the argument for the operators acting on registers $\bob \bob' \bob''$ proceeds identically). 
  1828		\begin{align}
  1829			&\sum_h \bra{\Delta} \left ( V_\alice \, M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h \, V_\alice^\dagger - (\tau^W_h)_{\alice''}  \right)^\dagger \left ( V_\alice \, M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h \, V_\alice^\dagger - (\tau^W_h)_{\alice''} \right) \ket{\Delta} \notag \\
  1830			&= 2 - 2 \Re \, \sum_h \bra{\Delta} V_\alice\, M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h \, V_\alice^\dagger  \, (\tau^W_h)_{\alice''} \ket{\Delta} \notag \\

  1832	\end{align}
  1833		where in the last line we used that $(\tau^W_h)_{\alice''} \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits} = (\tau^W_h)_{\bob''} \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}$.

  1835		\begin{align}
  1836		&  \, \sum_h \bra{\Delta} V_\alice \, M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h \, V_\alice^\dagger  \, \otimes (\tau^W_h)_{\bob''} \ket{\Delta}  \notag \\

  1838		&=  \E_u \sum_{a \in \F_q} \bra{\Delta} V_\alice \, M^{(\Pauli,W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} \, V_\alice^\dagger \, \otimes (\tau^W_{[g_h(u)=a]})_{\bob''} \ket{\Delta} \notag \\
  1839		&=  \E_u \sum_{a \in \F_q} \bra{\Delta} V_\alice \, M^{(\Pauli,W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} \, V_\alice^\dagger \, \otimes V_\bob  \, \tilde{M}^{W,\ind_m(u)}_a \, V_\bob^\dagger \ket{\Delta} \label{eq:qld-unitary-9}
  1840		\end{align}
  1841		where the equality in \Cref{eq:qld-unitary-9} follows from the identity in \Cref{eq:qld-unitary-6}, and the approximation in \Cref{eq:qld-unitary-8} follows from the following calculation:
  1842		\begin{align*}
  1843			& \E_u \sum_{\substack{h \neq h' : \\ g_h(u) = g_{h'}(u)}} \bra{\Delta} V_\alice \, M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h \, V_\alice^\dagger  \, \otimes (\tau^W_{h'})_{\bob''} \ket{\Delta}  \\

  1845			&\leq \frac{md}{q}\;.
  1846		\end{align*}

  1850		\begin{align*}
  1851			\text{\cref{eq:qld-unitary-9}} &\approx_{O(\delta_S^{1/4})} \E_u \sum_{a \in \F_q} \bra{\hat{\psi}} M^{(\Pauli,W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} \otimes \tilde{M}^{W,\ind_m(u)}_a \ket{\hat{\psi}} \\
  1852			&\geq 1 - O(\delta_S^{1/2})\;,
  1853		\end{align*}
  1854	        where the last line comes from \eqref{eq:qld-unitary-5}.
  1855		Together with \Cref{eq:qld-unitary-7}, 
  1856		\[
  1857		\text{\cref{eq:qld-unitary-7}} \leq O(\delta_S^{1/4} + md/q)\;.	
  1858		\]

  1860	\end{proof}

  1862	We now prove \Cref{thm:pauli-appendix}. 
  1863	\begin{proof}[Proof of \Cref{thm:pauli-appendix}]
  1864		Let $\strategy = (\psi,M)$ be a projective strategy for $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ that succeeds with probability at least $1 - \eps$, where $\ket{\psi}$ is a bipartite state on registers $\alice \bob$. As mentioned at the beginning of \Cref{sec:commutation}, we assume that the state $\ket{\psi}$ is padded with sufficiently many ancilla $\ket{0}$ qubits. Let $\phi_\alice$ be the following isometry mapping the register $\alice$ to the registers $\alice \alice' \alice''$ where $\alice'$ and $\alice''$ are isomorphic to $(\C^q)^{\otimes \nqubits}$:
  1865		\[
  1866			\phi_\alice: \ket{\theta}_\alice \mapsto V_\alice (\ket{\theta}_\alice \otimes (\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits})_{\alice' \alice''})
  1867		\]
  1868		where $V_\alice$ is the unitary acting on $\alice \alice' \alice''$ from \Cref{lem:qld-unitary}. Define the isometry $\phi_\bob$ analogously. \Cref{lem:qld-unitary} then implies that there exists a state $\ket{\aux}$ on registers $\alice \alice' \bob \bob'$ such that
  1869		\[
  1870			\left \| \phi_\alice \otimes \phi_\bob \ket{\psi} - \ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits} \right \|^2 \leq \delta_\qld
  1871		\]
  1872		and for $W \in \{X,Z\}$,
  1873		\[
  1874			\phi_\alice \, (M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h)_\alice \, \phi_\alice^\dagger \approx_{\delta_\qld} (\tau^W_h)_{\alice''} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \phi_\bob \, (M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h)_\bob \, \phi_\bob^\dagger \approx_{\delta_\qld} (\tau^W_h)_{\bob''}
  1875		\]
  1876		where the $\approx$ statement holds with respect to the state $\ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}$. This shows that $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ is a self-test for the strategy $\strategy^\pauli$ with robustness $\delta_\qld(\eps,m,d,q)$. We conclude the proof by making the identification of registers $\alice \alice'$ with $\alice'$ and $\bob \bob'$ with $\bob'$ to be consistent with the statement of \Cref{thm:pauli-appendix}.   1877	\end{proof}

   416	\paragraph{The strategy under analysis.}
   417	For the remainder of this chapter, as well as in
   418	Chapters~\ref{chap:qpbt-combining} and~\ref{chap:qpbt-extraction}, we fix
   419	an admissible parameter tuple $(q,m,d)$
   420	(Definition~\ref{def:admissible}) and a strategy
   421	$\mathcal{S} = (\ket{\psi}, M)$ for the game
   422	$\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Pauli}}_{(q,m,d)}$ that succeeds with probability
   423	at least $1 - \eps$, for some $\eps \geq 0$, where $\ket{\psi}$ is a
   424	bipartite state on registers $\mathsf{A}$ and $\mathsf{B}$ with associated
   425	Hilbert spaces $\hilb_{\mathsf{A}}$ and $\hilb_{\mathsf{B}}$. The symbol
   426	$M$ denotes the measurement operators of both players; which player is
   427	meant is indicated by the register on which the operator acts (for
   428	example, $M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a \ot \Id_{\mathsf{B}}$ indicates that
   429	$M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a$ is viewed as an operator acting on register
   430	$\mathsf{A}$).

   432	The analysis requires the measurements of $\mathcal{S}$ to be projective;
   433	the following lemma shows that this may be assumed without loss of
   434	generality.
   435	
   436	\begin{lemma}[Reduction to a projective strategy]
   437		\label{lem:projective-strategy-setup}
   438		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.exists_projective_padded_strategy}
   439		\leanok
   440		\uses{def:admissible, def:pauli-question-distribution, def:pauli-win-predicate, def:tensor-product-strategy, def:tensor-product-value, def:projective-strategy-general}
   441		Let $(q,m,d)$ be an admissible parameter tuple
   442		(Definition~\ref{def:admissible}) and let
   443		$\mathcal{S} = (\ket{\psi}, M)$ be a strategy for the game
   444		$\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Pauli}}_{(q,m,d)}$, where $\ket{\psi}$ is a
   445		bipartite state on registers $\mathsf{A}$ and $\mathsf{B}$. Then there
   446		exists a projective strategy
   447		(Definition~\ref{def:projective-strategy-general}) for
   448		$\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Pauli}}_{(q,m,d)}$ whose success probability
   449		equals that of $\mathcal{S}$ and whose state is the extension
   450		\[
   451			(\ket{\psi} \ot \ket{0\cdots 0} \ot \ket{0\cdots 0})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}}
   452		\]

   454		state $\ket{0}$, adjoined to each of the two registers.

   456	\begin{proof}
   457		\uses{thm:naimark, def:tensor-product-value, def:tensor-product-strategy}
   458		Naimark's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:naimark}), applied with the
   459		families of all of the first player's measurements on register
   460		$\mathsf{A}$ and all of the second player's on register $\mathsf{B}$,
   461		yields an auxiliary space and a projective sub-measurement replacing
   462		each family on each register, together with a product auxiliary state,
   463		such that every correlation
   464		$\bra{\psi} M^{x}_a \ot M^{y}_b \ket{\psi}$ of $\mathcal{S}$ is
   465		reproduced on the extended state. Each auxiliary space embeds into a
   466		register of finitely many qubits; extend each dilated sub-measurement
   467		to the enlarged register by adding to one fixed outcome both the
   468		projector onto the orthogonal complement of the embedded subspace and
   469		the residual projector of the sub-measurement. The outcome operators
   470		remain mutually orthogonal projectors, now summing to the identity,
   471		and no correlation changes: the complement projector annihilates the
   472		extended state, which is supported in the embedded subspace, and so
   473		does each residual projector, because for each question pair the
   474		reproduced correlations sum to one --- the original families being
   475		POVMs (Definition~\ref{def:tensor-product-strategy}) --- which forces
   476		the projector $\Id$ minus the sum of each dilated sub-measurement to
   477		have zero mass on the extended state. Finally, since the auxiliary
   478		state is a product state, a unitary acting on each player's ancilla
   479		qubits alone carries it to $\ket{0 \cdots 0} \ot \ket{0 \cdots 0}$;
   480		conjugating the projective measurements by the same unitaries
   481		preserves projectivity and all correlations. The success probability
   482		of a strategy is a linear combination of its correlations, weighted by
   483		the question distribution and the win predicate
   484		(Definition~\ref{def:tensor-product-value}), and is therefore
   485		unchanged.
   486	\end{proof}

    80	printed distinction is recovered from self-duality.  The chapter quantifies
    81	over arbitrary vectors, however, so that special case does not repair its
    82	statement.

    38	\section{Key theorem forms}
    39	
    40	Let $H_X$ and $H_Z$ be the positive contractions of the extraction proof, and
    41	let $\vartheta$ be a unit vector such that
    42	\[
    43	  \langle\vartheta,H_W\vartheta\rangle\geq1-\delta/2
    44	  \qquad (W\in\{X,Z\}).
    45	\]
    46	Since $(I-H_W)^2\geq0$,
    47	\[
    48	  H_W^2\geq2H_W-I,
    49	  \qquad
    50	  \langle\vartheta,H_W^2\vartheta\rangle\geq1-\delta.
    51	\]
    52	Also $\lVert(I-H_W)\vartheta\rVert^2\leq\delta$, whence
    53	\[
    54	  \lVert H_X\vartheta-H_Z\vartheta\rVert^2\leq4\delta.
    55	\]
    56	Together with $H_XH_Z$ equal to the EPR projection, these estimates give the
    57	required overlap bound, with constants absorbed into the stated
    58	$O(\sqrt\delta)$ error.
    59	
    60	For the final transfer, let $\phi\colon\mathcal H\to\mathcal K$ be an isometry
    61	and set $Q=\phi\phi^\dagger$.  If $N_h$ is the unitary-conjugated extension of
    62	a measurement operator $M_h$, then the exact identity is
    63	\[
    64	  \phi M_h\phi^\dagger=N_hQ=QN_h,
    65	\]
    66	not merely $N_h$.  Thus comparison of $N_h$ with an ideal projector must be
    67	combined with control of $(I-Q)\Delta$ on the ideal comparison state
    68	$\Delta$.

    70	\section{Numerical defects in the source proof}
    71	
    72	Lines~1715--1742 of
    73	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex}
    74	construct $H_X,H_Z$ and identify $H_XH_Z$ with the EPR projection.  The norm
    75	estimate at lines~1743--1750 gives
    76	$\lVert(I-H_W)\vartheta\rVert\leq\sqrt\delta$.  At lines~1753--1757 the
    77	source substitutes $\delta$ inside the reverse triangle inequality
    78	\cite[lines~1715--1783]{Ji2020MIPStar}.  That replacement is not valid for
    79	small $\delta$.  The desired lower bound on
    80	$\langle H_W^2\rangle$ follows directly from $H_W^2\geq2H_W-I$, as above.
    81	
    82	The triangle inequality yields
    83	\[
    84	  \lVert H_X\vartheta-H_Z\vartheta\rVert\leq2\sqrt\delta,
    85	\]
    86	so its square is at most $4\delta$.  Line~1761 instead bounds that square by
    87	$2\sqrt\delta$ without a stated restriction.  This inequality follows when
    88	$\delta\leq1/4$; for larger error the theorem is made trivial by enlarging the
    89	universal constant.  The same small-error split ensures that the projected
    90	vector defined at lines~1769--1773 is nonzero before it is normalized.  These
    91	are local numerical repairs and do not weaken the extraction conclusion.

    93	\section{The range-projection obligation}
    94	
    95	Lines~1827--1858 prove state-dependent closeness for the concrete operators
    96	obtained by conjugating the original measurement with the swap unitaries.
    97	Lines~1864--1875 then define isometries by adjoining EPR pairs and applying
    98	those unitaries, and immediately state the corresponding closeness for
    99	$\phi M_h\phi^\dagger$.  The omitted range projection makes this implication
   100	non-definitional \cite[lines~1827--1875]{Ji2020MIPStar}.
   101	
   102	Let $\Psi$ be the original state and suppose $\phi\Psi$ is close to the ideal
   103	state $\Delta$.  Since $Q\phi\Psi=\phi\Psi$ and $Q$ is a contraction, the
   104	triangle inequality bounds $(I-Q)\Delta$ by the state-extraction error.  Using
   105	$\phi M_h\phi^\dagger=N_hQ$, split
   106	\[
   107	  (N_hQ-T_h)\Delta
   108	  =(N_h-T_h)\Delta-N_h(I-Q)\Delta,
   109	\]
   110	where $T_h$ is the ideal Pauli projector.  Summing squared norms over $h$
   111	uses projectivity and orthogonality to keep the second term under control.
   112	The same argument is required for each player and each Pauli basis.
   113	
   114	This transfer is an open proof obligation for the next extraction stage.  It
   115	must be a theorem derived from the concrete swap unitaries, transformed-state
   116	estimate, and operator comparisons.  It must not be stored as a bridge field,
   117	residual assumption, or hypothesis of the source-labelled soundness theorem.

    38	\section{Key theorem forms}
    39	
    40	Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, let $\rho$ be an arbitrary
    41	density operator on $H$, and let $u\mapsto O^u$ be binary observables on $H$,
    42	indexed by $\mathbb F_2^t$.  The cited theorem assumes the averaged
    43	correlation estimate
    44	\[
    45	  \mathop{\mathbb E}_{u,v}
    46	  \operatorname{Tr}\!\left(O^u O^v O^{u+v}\rho\right) \geq 1-\delta.
    47	\]
    48	It produces an auxiliary space $H'$, a unit vector $\mathrm{anc}\in H'$, and
    49	binary observables $L^u$ on $H\otimes H'$ satisfying, with
    50	$\rho'=\rho\otimes|\mathrm{anc}\rangle\langle\mathrm{anc}|$,
    51	\[
    52	  L^uL^v=L^{u+v}
    53	  \quad\text{for every }u,v.
    54	\]
    55	Moreover,
    56	\[
    57	  \mathop{\mathbb E}_{u}
    58	  \operatorname{Tr}\!\left((L^u-O^u\otimes I_{H'})^\dagger
    59	    (L^u-O^u\otimes I_{H'})\,\rho'\right)\leq\delta.
    60	\]
    61	In particular, $L^0=I$: exact linearity gives $(L^0)^2=L^0$, while an
    62	observable is invertible.
    63	
    64	The chapter needs a parameterized version.  For each pair $(x,z)$ it applies
    65	the theorem to $(r,s)\mapsto O^{x,z,r,s}$.  Since the provider theorem accepts
    66	the actual nonnegative defect on each fiber, no assumption that a fiber defect
    67	is at most one, and no good--bad fiber split, is needed.  One must still
    68	formulate the finite common-extension step that makes the auxiliary space
    69	uniform over $(x,z)$.

    71	\section{Comparison with the quoted statement}
    72	
    73	Lines~711--725 of
    74	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex} quote the
    75	linearity theorem.  The displayed hypothesis correctly averages over both

   822	\begin{remark}
   823	  \label{rmk:tm_fields}
   824	  Throughout this paper, whenever we refer to Turing machines that perform
   825	  computations with elements of a field $\F_q$ for an admissible field size $q =
   826	  2^k$, we mean that that the Turing machines are representing elements of
   827	  $\F_q$ as vectors in $\{0,1\}^{k}$ using the basis specified by the
   828	  algorithm of Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_basis} and performing arithmetic as
   829	  described in Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}.
   830	\end{remark}
   831	
   832	\subsection{Polynomials and the low-degree code}
   833	\label{sec:ld-encoding}
   834	
   835	In this section, we introduce some basic definitions about polynomials over finite fields. 
   836	An $m$-variate polynomial $f$ over $\F_q$ is a function of the form
   837	\[
   838		f(x_1,\ldots,x_m) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}^m} c_\alpha
   839	  x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_m^{\alpha_m}
   840	\]
   841	where $\{c_\alpha\}$ is a collection of coefficients in $\F_q$.
   842	We say that $f$ has \emph{individual degree (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if
   843	$\alpha_i \leq d $ for all $1\leq i\leq m$, and that it has \emph{total degree
   844	  (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if $\sum_i \alpha_i \leq d$.
   845	(Affine) \emph{multilinear} polynomials are polynomials with individual degree
   846	$1$.
   847	
   848	Low-degree polynomials play an important role in this paper.
   849	For one, the classical and quantum low-degree tests of \Cref{sec:ldt} are
   850	nonlocal games that efficiently certify that the players' answers are consistent
   851	with low-degree polynomials.
   852	Low-degree polynomials are also crucial in the probabilistically checkable
   853	proofs (PCP) construction that are used in ``answer reduction'' transformation
   854	(\Cref{sec:ans}).
   855	
   856	We recall the Schwartz-Zippel lemma: 
   857	
   858	\begin{lemma}[Schwartz-Zippel lemma~\cite{Sch80,Zip79}]
   859	  \label{lem:schwartz-zippel}
   860	  Let $f, g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ be two unequal polynomials with total degree at most $d$. Then
   861	  \begin{equation*}
   862	    \Pr_{x \sim \F_q^m}[f(x) = g(x)] \leq d/q\;.
   863	  \end{equation*}
   864	\end{lemma}
   865	
   866	
   867	\paragraph{The low-degree code.}
   868	The Schwartz-Zippel lemma implies that the set of low-degree polynomials form an
   869	error-correcting code with good distance, which we call the \emph{low-degree
   870	  code}.\footnote{It is also known as the \emph{generalized Reed-Muller code} in
   871	  the coding theory literature.}
   872	
   873	Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$.
   874	For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ define the following $m$-variate multilinear
   875	polynomial over $\F_q$:
   876	\[
   877		\ind_{m,y}(x) = \prod_{i: y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i: y_i = 0} (1 - x_i) \;.
   878	\]
   879	Here, we identify $\{0,1\}$ as a subset of $\F_q$.
   880	Notice that, when restricted to the subcube $\{0,1\}^m$, $\ind_{m, y}$ is zero
   881	everywhere except for when $x = y$.
   882	For $a\in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y\in \{0,1\}^m$
   883	(identifying the latter set with $\{1,\ldots,M\}$ using, say, the lexicographic
   884	ordering on strings).

   335		\[

   383	\begin{remark}[Norm conventions in the robustness bound]\label{rem:pauli-robustness-form}
   384		The proof above, following the source, establishes the first conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli} in the squared form $\| \phi_{\mathrm{A}} \ot \phi_{\mathrm{B}} \ket{\psi} - \ket{\mathrm{aux}} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M} \|^2 \leq \delta_{\mathrm{qld}}$, whereas the theorem bounds the unsquared norm by $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}(\eps,m,d,q)$. The two are reconciled by replacing the exponent $b$ with $b/2$ and enlarging $a$, since the class of functions $a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ is closed under square roots up to such adjustments of the universal constants. Similarly, the closing sentence of the source proof asserts constants $a > 1$ and $0 < b < 1$, while Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli} requires only $a \geq 1$ and $0 < b < 1$; the former implies the latter.
   385	\end{remark}
